§9.6.7 Struck and Replaced Values

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

tables-struck-and-replaced-values · tables redline ocr failure-mode

✅ Normative

A cell holding a struck value and its replacement MUST render both, struck first — ~~1.316~~ 1.335 — and MUST NOT merge them into one figure. The ~~ MUST cover exactly the glyphs struck on the page: 1.~~316~~ 335 when only the digits are crossed out.

A cell holds an old value crossed out plus its replacement. A text layer joins them without a trace:

page shows:  1.316 (struck)  1.335
text layer:  1.316335        ← this number does not exist on the page

That is the worst outcome available on a table: not a drop and not a garble, but a fabricated number that looks entirely plausible and that nothing downstream can catch. Struck cells MUST be read from the rendered page, never from the text layer — see Cell Text Fidelity§9.6.3.

Writing the cell

  • A struck value and its replacement MUST be rendered ~~old~~ new, which keeps the two readings distinct and marks which one is superseded.
  • Where the page marks the change with an underline instead of a strike, the replacement MUST be rendered <u>1.335</u>, recording what is actually drawn.
  • A handwritten correction over a printed value MUST use the same markup — see Handwriting and Stamps§9.6.5. A printed strikethrough and a pen stroke are the same act, so a consumer never has to tell them apart.
  • The output MUST NOT restructure the table into "Previous" and "Current" columns. Where the page itself prints the old and new figures in separate tables or columns, each MUST be rendered where it appears rather than folded into one cell.

✅ Sample — strike

Every Current Rates figure is struck through, with its live replacement in the Proposed Rates tables alongside: 54 struck values across two tables. Each struck value is wrapped in ~~…~~, and the four blocks stay four tables.

Note what the page itself does: it splits old and new into parallel tables, so the replacement is not in the same cell. The output follows the page and does not fold them together.

The strike span mirrors the printed strike

Where the strike starts and stops is printed information, and the markup carries it: exactly the struck glyphs, no more, no less.

whole value struck:      1.316 (all struck)  335        →  ~~1.316~~ 335
only the digits struck:  1.316 (316 struck)  335        →  1.~~316~~ 335

The unstruck 1. sits outside the ~~, because that is where it sits on the page. Nothing is reconstructed and nothing is invented — the prefix is transcribed because it is printed and was never struck.

1.~~316~~ 335 gives a reader everything needed to arrive at 1.335 without the output asserting it. The 1. is printed, unstruck, and therefore still part of the value; the replacement digits follow. The reading falls out of the transcription instead of being asserted on top of it.

That is why the span must be exact. ~~1.316~~ 335 for a page that only struck 316 throws away the prefix a reader needs, and 1.~~316~~ 335 for a page that struck the whole value claims ink that is not there. Both are losses, in opposite directions.

One struck cell puts the column in play

Strikes are thin and reproduce badly at page zoom, so a struck cell is easy to miss. One struck cell means the column is a redline column: every other cell in it MUST be read for a strike before the column is rendered.

Redline in prose

  • Deleted text MUST be rendered ~~…~~ and inserted underlined text <u>…</u>, each over exactly the printed span.
  • Where colour distinguishes revisions or authors, the colour MUST be preserved as well. Insertion MUST NOT be inferred from colour alone where the page marks nothing else.

✅ Sample — an interlineated court rule

Paragraph (4): [Deleted.] struck through in red, followed by red underlined replacement text; everything above it is plain black. Strike and underline already carry the revision, so the red adds nothing a strike and an underline do not.

Expected Markdown · paragraph (4)

(4) [Deleted.] Unless otherwise agreed to by the parties or otherwise provided by court order or by law, only the witness, the parties, their respective counsel including such counsel's staff, experts identified pursuant to Rule 4:1(b)(4)(A), and those involved with the administration of the deposition (such as court reporters and translators) may attend the deposition, given the private nature of discovery. Counsel of record for the parties and counsel for any non-party deponent must timely confer regarding any other person's attendance at a deposition

✅ Sample — insertions marked by colour alone


Source: Advisory Committee on Civil Rules (U.S. Courts), Proposed Amendments to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 30(b)(6) (public domain)

Proposed rule text: deletions (then, make this designation) struck through in black, insertions in red with no underline. Without the colour the insertions become indistinguishable from the settled text, so the colour is kept. The colour is written as <font color="red"> around the inserted words, as Text Colors§7.3.12 requires.

Expected Markdown · paragraph (6)

(6) Notice or Subpoena Directed to an Organization. In its notice or subpoena, a party may name as the deponent a public or private corporation, a partnership, an association, a governmental agency, or other entity and must describe with reasonable particularity the matters for examination. The named organization must then designate one or more officers, directors, or managing agents, or designate other persons who consent to testify on its behalf; and it may set out the matters on which each person designated will testify. Before or promptly after the notice or subpoena is served, the serving party and the organization must confer in good faith about the matters for examination. A subpoena must advise a nonparty organization of its duty to confer with the serving party and to designate each person who will testify make this designation. The persons designated must testify about information known or reasonably available to the organization. This paragraph (6) does not preclude a deposition by any other procedure allowed by these rules.
